\title{When Modal Contact Rows Fail in Fixed-Budget XPBD:\\
  Diagnosis and an Operating Guide}

\author{Anonymous Author(s)}

\begin{abstract}
Rigid-body XPBD engines already resolve contacts and joints, and a small global
modal state ($16$--$24$ amplitudes) is an attractive way to give a stiff prop
low-cost vibration without a full nodal or tetrahedral deformable. We show that
inserting this shared state directly into a two-way unilateral contact row need
not keep modal storage within the measured rigid-side supply once the host runs
only a few local iterations per substep. Across three scenes, two relaxations
and four schedules, our tested XPBD implementation overdraws that supply by up
to $4.4\times10^{7}$~J, augmented-Lagrangian and implicit implementations by at
most $6.7$~J in $3$ of $24$ cells and never, respectively. An iteration ladder,
equal-row-count schedules and a within-host weight swap trace the amplification
to the modal contact-row weight: the stiffness-aware implicit form removes the
overdraw in every injecting cell while still retaining $0.70$--$0.89\times$ the
converged modal energy wherever the substep resolves the retained band, and
where the weight is fixed the budget is better spent on iterations than on
substeps or a block solve. For hosts that
still cannot converge the row, a cumulative modal-storage projection enforces
its accounting bound unconditionally (Prop.~\ref{prop:guarantee}, roundoff
floor in all $90$ measured cells). Holding the contact-observed surface fixed,
it cuts the penetration it opens from $2.4$--$47.6\times$ the truncated solve's
own to $1.0$--$6.3\times$ (both relaxations; Table~\ref{tab:validity} shows the
$0.7$ rows) without removing it: the truncated row opens the residue, which the
projection still amplifies.
\end{abstract}

% =====================================================================
\section{Introduction}
% =====================================================================
A developer building an interactive scene on a rigid-body XPBD
engine~\citep{mueller2020xpbd} already has a solver resolving contacts and joints
under a small, fixed local-iteration budget. To make a stiff prop such
as a shelf, a table, or a ledge ring when struck, the heavyweight option is a
full nodal or tetrahedral deformable with thousands of online coordinates; the
lighter one is a precomputed modal basis of $16$--$24$ global amplitudes
$\mathbf{q}$ capturing the low-frequency bending of a stiff, small-displacement
body~\citep{james2002dyrt,hauser2003,peng2024reduced}: a handful of extra
runtime numbers, offline precomputation, one host stepping everything. This
paper is written for that developer, and does not argue XPBD against another
solver.

The difficulty lies in the contact. In the real-time precedent the modal prop
is driven \emph{one way}: an external filter reads detected contact events and
rings the modes with no back-reaction~\citep{coevoet2020distant},
double-counting the interface energy and leaving the prop's deformation unable
to change how it is supported. The \emph{two-way} alternative resolves rigid
and modal unknowns through one shared contact multiplier~\citep{zheng2011}, so
a heavier load bends the support and the bent support redistributes the load.
But every support contact touches the same global $\mathbf{q}$, making the
contact-row graph dense on the modes, and a host running a few local iterations
per substep need not converge it. We take the row as given: the velocity-level
law of~\citet{zheng2011}
($C^{n+1}\!\approx\!C^{n}+h\,\mathbf{J}\mathbf{u}^{n+1}$, same Jacobian and
multiplier), narrowed to normal rows with $e{=}0$ and transcribed into the
host's positional-impulse idiom. That transcription is not neutral:
\citet{zheng2011} resolve against the implicit step's reduced effective mass,
whereas a position-based host weights the row by an inverse mass, which for
mass-normalized modes is $\mathbf{I}$: the natural thing to write on this host,
no contribution of ours, and the lever of \S\ref{sec:kconv}. What does it cost
at a normal budget, and what should one do about it?

Finite-iteration coupling across a partition boundary can inject spurious
energy even when every subsystem is individually
passive~\citep{wei2026earlyterm}, and velocity-level frictional contact
spanning rigid and reduced deformable bodies, with the energy artifacts of
iterative solvers named, goes back at least to~\citet{kaufman2008}. Missing is
a quantitative account of the present case, unilateral contact-to-modal
transfer in a fixed-budget host, together with an operating guide; this paper
supplies both.

\paragraph*{Contributions.}
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textbf{A practitioner workflow and its failure.} Treated as the workflow
  it is, adding a compact modal state to a fixed-budget XPBD host overdraws the
  measured rigid-side supply by up to $4.4\times10^{7}$~J at interactive
  budgets across three scenes, two relaxations and four schedules
  (\S\ref{sec:matrix}), with augmented-Lagrangian and implicit implementations
  as milder controls, a gravity/no-contact accounting audit, and a
  deterministic perturbation ensemble.
\item \textbf{Mechanism and an operating guide.} An iteration ladder,
  equal-row-count schedules, warm starting, mode truncation and an in-host
  block-condensation ablation localize the amplification to the stiffness-blind
  modal weight in the shared row, exposed rather than caused by a truncated
  solve (\S\ref{sec:kconv}), giving an ordered rule: a stiffness-aware weight
  where the architecture allows, otherwise iterations and a verified basis
  rather than more substeps or a block solve.
\item \textbf{A last-resort guardrail and its price.} A cumulative
  modal-storage bound funded by the measured rigid-side loss and enforced by a
  scalar projection of the realized state (\S\ref{sec:bound}): a deliberately
  minimal fail-safe, guaranteed unconditionally (Prop.~\ref{prop:guarantee},
  roundoff floor in all $90$ measured cells), at a measured cost to contact
  validity (\S\ref{sec:validity}).
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph*{Related work.} Rigid XPBD~\citep{mueller2020xpbd}, interactive modal
deformation and velocity-level modal contact~\citep{james2002dyrt,hauser2003,%
zheng2011,kaufman2008}, and reduced XPBD~\citep{peng2024reduced} set the stage;
the last uses modes as a deformation surrogate, whereas here modal
amplitudes enter as contact DOFs driven by the shared multiplier
(cf.~penalty contact without a shared
multiplier~\citep{zobel2025unity}). The guardrail adapts energy-tank
control~\citep{hannaford2002,franken2011,rath2008} rather than inventing a
mechanism: it keeps the tank-and-observer structure but funds the tank from the
measured rigid-side loss rather than from the port it regulates, and scales the
realized state rather than a force, since a fixed-budget solver commits its
multipliers before the excess is observable. That separates it from
total-energy projection~\citep{dinev2018fepr}, bidirectional total-energy
tracking~\citep{you2026energy}, and the structural finite-budget passivity of
bilateral couplings~\citep{wei2026earlyterm}. Two schemes are closer still:
passive midpoint integration~\citep{kim2017pmi} attains passivity by modifying
the integrator, whereas the host here is assumed fixed and its integrator and
contact solve left untouched; and frame-rate energy
clamping~\citep{su2009energy} caps energy per frame against a prescribed
budget, whereas ours is cumulative and measured from the rigid-side loss, which
lets a substep deposit more than it earns while the running total stays
admissible.

% =====================================================================
\section{The row and the invariant it must respect}
\label{sec:row}
% =====================================================================
Let $\mathbf{q}\in\mathbb{R}^{r}$ be mass-normalized modal amplitudes of the
supporting body, so its modal mechanical energy is
$\Emod=\tfrac12\dot{\mathbf{q}}^{\!\top}\dot{\mathbf{q}}
      +\tfrac12\mathbf{q}^{\!\top}\mathbf{K}\mathbf{q}$.
A support-contact row between a rigid corner at world height $y_c$ and the
deformed surface has gap
\begin{equation}
C \;=\; y_c \;-\; \bigl(y_{\mathrm{rest}} + \mathbf{U}_y^{\!\top}\mathbf{q}\bigr),
\qquad C \ge 0,\; \lambda \ge 0,\; C\lambda = 0,
\label{eq:row}
\end{equation}
with $\partial C/\partial\mathbf{q}=-\mathbf{U}_y$, so one multiplier $\lambda$
drives both the rigid body and the modal amplitudes. Equation~\eqref{eq:row} is
the transcription discussed above rather than a new law: one row, instantiated
at every support contact in every substep ($48$ on the shelf, $40$ on the
ledge, $200$ on the table), all sharing the one modal state $\mathbf{q}$.

\paragraph*{The invariant.} The energy stored in the modal subsystem must never
exceed the measured gross rigid-side loss of \eqref{eq:derig} below,
cumulatively over the run:
\begin{equation}
\Emod^{\,n} - \Emod^{\,0}
\;\;\le\;\;
\eta \sum_{k\le n} \max\!\bigl(\dErig^{\,k},\,0\bigr),
\qquad \eta\in(0,1].
\label{eq:invariant}
\end{equation}
The transfer efficiency $\eta$ sets how much of the measured loss may be spent;
every experiment here runs $\eta=1$, the least restrictive admissible value, so
no result depends on tuning it. Being cumulative rather than per-step, the bound
lets a substep deposit more than it earns provided the running total stays
within budget, so a legitimate ring persists.

\paragraph*{Definitions.} Modal storage is the mechanical energy of the reduced
state above, with $\Emod^{\,0}=0$: every scene starts from an undeformed,
resting support, so even the run's own settling transient must be funded by the
reservoir. The supply is
\begin{equation}
\dErig^{\,k} \;=\; \bigl(E_{\mathrm{rig}}^{k,-} - E_{\mathrm{rig}}^{k,+}\bigr)
                 \;+\; W_g^{\,k},
\qquad
W_g^{\,k}=\sum_b m_b\,\mathbf{g}\!\cdot\!\bigl(\mathbf{x}_b^{k,+}-\mathbf{x}_b^{k,-}\bigr),
\label{eq:derig}
\end{equation}
where $E_{\mathrm{rig}}=\sum_b\bigl[\tfrac12 m_b\|\mathbf{v}_b\|^2
+\tfrac12\boldsymbol{\omega}_b^{\!\top}\mathbf{I}_b\boldsymbol{\omega}_b\bigr]$
is purely kinetic (over all dynamic bodies, not only those in contact) and
$\pm$ are the ends of substep $k$. We call this the \textbf{measured
gross rigid-side loss}: a loss, not a dissipation, since it also counts
legitimate rigid-to-modal transfer and rigid--rigid losses elsewhere in the
scene, an envelope on what contact dissipated rather than a measurement of it
(\S\ref{sec:limits}). Gravity enters only through $W_g$, so free ballistic
motion registers zero supply and only an inelastic velocity change funds the
reservoir; substep endpoints tile the timeline exactly, so no rigid energy
change escapes the accounting.

\paragraph*{Two diagnostics.} The right-hand side of \eqref{eq:invariant} is
the measured loss of \eqref{eq:derig}, never a tuned constant or a fraction of
incident energy, and it constrains a scalar reservoir rather than a contact
port, so the bound is neither port passivity nor a signed per-interface
statement (\S\ref{sec:limits} measures what its gross sum recycles). Two
diagnostics stay distinct: the incident-energy ratio $R=$~peak modal energy /
peak incident rigid KE, a severity measure read once per frame, and the signed
margin of \eqref{eq:invariant} in joules, the invariant proper, evaluated
against the running supply at every substep commit. They need not flag the same
cells, and because the ledger sees intra-frame excursions the frame sample
misses, a cell's margin may exceed its reported peak modal energy.

% =====================================================================
\section{The failure at a fixed budget}
% =====================================================================
All solver-behaviour measurements come from one machine (Apple M4, CPU,
CPython 3.12), since chaotic contact stacks diverge across architectures under
floating-point reassociation. Every number is frozen with its command and commit
in the supplemental archive, which ships the per-cell CSVs and configurations
behind every figure and table here, a code snapshot, a pinned environment and a
smoke test; the supplementary video shows the comparisons at true scale.


\subsection{One row, three implementations, the same 24 cells}
\label{sec:matrix}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.63\textwidth]{fig_xpbd_map.pdf}
\caption{Our tested XPBD implementation over the 24-cell sweep (3 scenes
$\times$ relaxation $\{0.7,1.0\}$ $\times$ budget), governor OFF.
\textbf{Left:} $R$ = peak modal energy / peak incident rigid KE (top) and the
signed margin of \eqref{eq:invariant} in joules (bottom; $>0$ violates); the
two need not flag the same cells ($8/24$ vs $9/24$), itself a result.
\textbf{Right:} a control strip for the three implementations (one of each,
neither compliance- nor cost-matched): a scale gap rather than a ranking,
$4.4\times10^{7}$~J vs.\ $\le6.7$~J vs.\ $0$, with an accounting audit putting
the control floor below $10^{-3}$~J, so $6.7$~J is real injection (full 72-cell
heatmap in the supplement).}
\label{fig:matrix}
\end{figure*}

We drive an impactor into a modally reduced support in three scenes (a shelf
board, a ledge slab, and a $2.2\times1.1$~m table, the last two following the
layouts of \citet{coevoet2020distant}) and sweep modal relaxation and the
local budget (iterations $\times$ substeps) over
$\{4{\times}1, 8{\times}2, 16{\times}4, 32{\times}8\}$. Per scene, as
shelf\,/\,ledge\,/\,table: Young's modulus $0.5$\,/\,$10$\,/\,$1.1$~GPa;
density $600$\,/\,$500$\,/\,$770$~kg\,m$^{-3}$; impactor $6$\,/\,$50$\,/\,$5$~kg
dropped $0.50$\,/\,$0.80$\,/\,$0.50$~m; realized modal rank
$16$\,/\,$16$\,/\,$24$, of which $6$\,/\,$4$\,/\,$14$ form a stiff cluster;
retained modes spanning $20$~Hz--$24.7$~kHz, $118$~Hz--$191$~kHz, and
$4.7$~Hz--$5.2$~kHz. At the deployed $h$ these give
$\omega_{\max}h\approx1.3{\times}10^{3}$, $1.0{\times}10^{4}$ and
$2.7{\times}10^{2}$, so \eqref{eq:overweight} turns on: the two scenes that
inject on the position-based host carry modes three to four orders above the
substep rate; the table does not, though the augmented-Lagrangian host
overdraws there, so \eqref{eq:overweight} is necessary and not sufficient. The
hosts are
XPBD~\citep{macklin2016xpbd}, AVBD~\citep{giles2025avbd} (from vertex block
descent~\citep{chen2024vbd}), and a sequential-impulse realization in the sense
of~\citet{catto2005iterative}, made implicit in the modal block, all pinned to
a frame step $\Delta t{=}1/120$~s subdivided into $S$ substeps of $h{=}\Delta
t/S$, so every cell advances the same physical time per frame and all
step-dependent quantities are formed at $h$. They share per-substep contact
regeneration, Rayleigh damping, an implicit-midpoint modal restoring step and
$\eta{=}1$, and differ in the unknown solved for (position,
position\,+\,multiplier, or velocity), the modal contact weight, warm start and
relaxation (full table in the supplement). Relaxation is inert on the impulse
host (its implicit weight needs none), so its two rows are bit-identical, and
warm start is as-deployed ($\lambda\!\leftarrow\!0$ every substep for the
position-based host, carried duals for the others) and not the lever:
warm-starting it leaves the footprint unchanged (the same $8/24$ cells, worst
$1.20\times10^{5}$) and is worse, not better, at $4{\times}1$
(Fig.~\ref{fig:kconv}a). The decisive difference is the contact-row weight,
isolated with a within-host control in \S\ref{sec:kconv}.

\paragraph*{Equal row evaluations, unequal outcome.} A cell costs $K\!\cdot\!S$
row evaluations per frame, so the budget axis conflates two refinements that
are neither interchangeable nor equally costly. At $32$ row evaluations on the
shelf drop, spent as iterations ($K{=}32,S{=}1$) the ratio is $0.300$ and
\eqref{eq:invariant} holds; spent as substeps ($K{=}4,S{=}8$) it is $3.13$,
overdrawing by $481$~J. Substeps do reduce the ratio (Fig.~\ref{fig:kconv}a),
roughly $2200\times$ over the same range, but in this equal-row shelf
comparison they are the less cost-effective refinement; we claim the inversion
for this row, not for constraints generally.

Figure~\ref{fig:matrix} shows the outcome. The position-based host exceeds
$R=1$ in $8$ of $24$ cells, worst $1.2\times10^{5}$ (ledge, relaxation $1.0$,
$4{\times}1$: peak modal energy $4.44\times10^{7}$~J against an incident
$371$~J), the augmented-Lagrangian host in $2$ of $24$ (worst $1.70$), so
neither is unconditionally benign; the ordering also inverts with the scene,
the augmented-Lagrangian host being the worse on the table ($1.70$ against
$0.37$).

\paragraph*{The ratio is not the invariant.} We also measure
\eqref{eq:invariant} directly on all three hosts, ungoverned (the accounting is
forced inert; trajectories are bit-identical). The diagnostics disagree: the
position-based host violates it in $9$ of $24$ against $R>1$ in $8$, the
augmented-Lagrangian host in $3$ against $2$, the implicit host in neither
($0/24$, at the roundoff floor). Magnitude orders the failures: the
position-based overdraw reaches $4.4\times10^{7}$~J, seven orders beyond the
largest augmented-Lagrangian one ($6.7$~J, at the starved $4{\times}1$ table
corner) and the implicit host's exact zero. A resting-contact, no-impact audit
puts the augmented-Lagrangian and implicit control floor below $10^{-3}$~J, so
that overdraft is real impact-driven injection rather than accounting noise.
The position-based host has no small floor: at a starved budget it already
injects $10^{3}$~J from resting settling alone, the same failure without an
impact event rather than a separate one.

\subsection{The position-based amplification is a truncation artifact}
\label{sec:kconv}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.68\textwidth]{fig_operating_envelope.pdf}
\caption{The XPBD operating envelope (our tested position-based host, governor
OFF). \textbf{(a)}~Injection $R$ vs.\ local iterations $K$ on a deterministic
shelf drop ($S{=}1$): $R$ decays monotonically toward the implicit reference
($0.273$), crossing the incident-energy threshold between $K{=}16$ and $24$;
annotations mark the $32{\times}1$-vs-$4{\times}8$ equal-row pair and warm
starting. \textbf{(b)}~The end-of-substep gap converges with $K$, so the
falling ratio tracks the row converging rather than one scalar shrinking.
\textbf{(c)}~Serial per-row support projection (the path used here) vs.\ joint
block condensation (supplement E6a-1), both scenes: the serial path holds by
$16{\times}4$--$32{\times}1$, condensation injects where it holds.}
\label{fig:kconv}
\end{figure*}

Figure~\ref{fig:kconv} isolates the local iteration budget. Two references
recur below: the \emph{implicit reference}, the implicit realization run to
$K{=}500$ (the same code path, only more iterations), and the \emph{XPBD
self-reference}, the position-based host run to $K{=}500$ against itself. The
position-based host falls monotonically from $2.96\times10^{4}$ at $K{=}1$ to
$0.300$ at $K{=}32$, approaching the implicit reference $0.2735$, the gap
$|\text{XPBD}-\text{reference}|$ shrinking from $2.96\times10^{4}$ to
$2.7\times10^{-2}$, while the implicit realization moves only in the fourth
decimal across $K=2\ldots500$ (max$-$min $6.8\times10^{-4}$).

A falling energy ratio could shrink coincidentally; measuring the constraint
directly resolves that, with the two complementarity conditions read in their
own units. End-of-substep penetration falls from $27.9$~mm at $K{=}1$ to
$3.6\,\mu$m by $K{=}64$, where it saturates, while the multiplier surviving on
separated rows (force where the gap is open, in units of the steady-state
median) rises from $84\times$ to $139\times$ through $K{=}24$ and collapses to
zero only at $K{=}64$. The energy crossing at $K\approx24$ therefore coincides
with the gap converging, not with complementarity holding: the multiplier side
clears a rung later. These measurements concern the position-based host only,
the implicit realization being converged at $K{=}2$.

\paragraph*{Self-convergence stops short of the reference.} Running the
position-based host to $K\!=\!500$ against itself does not close the gap: its
ratio plateaus by $K\approx64$ at $0.2996$, a fixed point $2.6\times10^{-2}$
above the reference's $0.2735$, not a tail. The state agrees no better: the
deflection peak matches to $2.4\%$, the trajectories differing by $6.8$~mm
($34\%$ of the reference's peak). The two hosts converge to different discrete
solutions, as expected of two discretizations of one law, and the sweep
separates a truncation pathology that convergence removes from a
discretization difference it does not.

\paragraph*{The contact-row weight is the lever.} The three-host comparison of
\S\ref{sec:matrix} confounds solver family with the modal contact-row weight; a
within-host control separates them. Three quantities must be kept apart: the
\emph{compliance} $\tilde\alpha{=}\alpha/h^2$, XPBD's regularizer added to the
row denominator (the support row is near-rigid, $\alpha_{\rm sup}{=}10^{-8}$,
and the symplectic step's separate modal-elastic constraint carries its own
$\tilde\alpha_e$); the \emph{modal inverse mass} $\mathbf{W}_q$ [kg$^{-1}$]
multiplying the Jacobian; and the \emph{modal mobility}
$\mathbf{U}_y^{\!\top}\mathbf{W}_q\mathbf{U}_y$, the modal share of that
denominator. The lever is $\mathbf{W}_q$, not either compliance.

With mass-normalized modes the deployed row uses the \emph{true}
$\mathbf{W}_q{=}\mathbf{M}_q^{-1}{=}\mathbf{I}$, so its mobility is independent
of $\omega_i$: the row is stiffness-blind. The stiffness-aware alternative uses
the effective inverse inertia
$\mathbf{W}_q{=}(\mathbf{M}_q{+}h\mathbf{D}_q{+}h^2\mathbf{K}_q)^{-1}$, per
mode $1/(1{+}h d_i{+}(\omega_i h)^2)$. Holding the position-based host fixed in
every other respect (position-level unknown, warm start, relaxation,
per-substep contact regeneration, symplectic modal step) and replacing only
$\mathbf{W}_q$ removes the overdraw in every injecting cell:
$8/24\to0/24$, the deployed ledge $4{\times}1$ falling from
$R=1.2\times10^{5}$ to $8\times10^{-5}$ and never worse at any budget (the
baseline arm reproduces Fig.~\ref{fig:matrix} exactly).

The swap contains the injection without simply deleting the response, provided
the substep resolves the retained band. At the injecting shelf $8{\times}2$
cell it stores $5.57$~J against the implicit reference's $7.92$~J
($0.70\times$, where the deployed row stores $1555.6$~J), and across the shelf
and table at $16{\times}4$--$32{\times}8$ it holds $0.70$--$0.89\times$ the
deployed row's own converged energy. The ledge is the exception that proves the
rule: at $\omega_{\max}h\!\approx\!10^{4}$ the same weight damps even its
softest retained mode to $2.5\%$ mobility, so there a stiffness-aware weight
and a step-aware basis are not separable choices. The mechanism is their ratio:
the deployed row over-estimates how freely mode $i$ moves within a substep by
\begin{equation}
\label{eq:overweight}
  [\mathbf{W}_q^{\rm depl}]_{ii}\big/[\mathbf{W}_q^{\rm impl}]_{ii}
  \;=\; 1+h d_i+(\omega_i h)^2 \;\approx\;(\omega_i h)^2
  \quad (\omega_i h\!\gg\!1),
\end{equation}
so a stiff mode is displaced as if it had no restoring stiffness, and the
restoring step values that over-displacement at
$\tfrac12\omega_i^2\Delta q_i^2$. On the ledge
($\omega_{\max}h\!\approx\!10^{4}$, \S\ref{sec:matrix})
\eqref{eq:overweight} reaches $\sim\!10^{8}$ on the stiffest retained mode.
The failure is thus a property of a stiffness-blind row weight at
$\omega_i h\!\gg\!1$ rather than of the fixed budget as such, consistent with
the iteration ladder, the equal-row comparison, and the implicit host's
convergence at $K{=}2$.

Convergence therefore largely cures the amplification (more iterations, the
implicit realization, or merely its contact-row weight), so the bound of
\S\ref{sec:bound} is no substitute for it and targets only the regime where
neither escape is available. That regime is common: interactive position-based
solvers run near $1{\times}8$--$2{\times}4$~\citep{macklin2019small}, well below
the $K\!\ge\!24$ this scene needs, and there the position-based host violates
\eqref{eq:invariant} in all six deployed cells (worst $R=2282$, on $8$ row
evaluations) while the others match the sweep ($1/6$, $0/6$).

\paragraph*{Condensing the shared rows is not the fix.} What converges the row
is the iteration budget, not how the shared rows are scheduled: replacing the
serial per-row support projection with a joint block condensation (modal
weight, restoring step, budget and warm start fixed; Fig.~\ref{fig:kconv}(c))
does not remove the injection. It is comparable at the
starved $4{\times}1$ corner and markedly worse wherever the serial path holds
($R=12.5$ and $66.5$ at $32{\times}1$ on shelf and ledge, against $0.30$ and
$0.09$; the budget axis is ordered by schedule, not by the $K\!\cdot\!S$ cost,
so $32{\times}1$ is half the cost of $16{\times}4$). In the two scenes and four
budgets tested, condensation exposes a worse convergence path, not a cure; we
do not claim this of block solves in general.

\paragraph*{Robustness of the failure.} The catastrophic cells are not a
knife-edge. For each worst cell, the equal-row pair and the guardrail cell we
run $16$ paired deterministic perturbations ($12$ physical, $4$
contact-row-order permutations; supplement). Every injecting cell overdraws in
all $16$, the sign never flips, and the $4.4\times10^{7}$~J anchor sits near the
top of a $2.2$--$4.5\times10^{7}$~J band; this establishes local insensitivity,
not generalization. Mode truncation
localizes the amplification without removing it: excluding the stiff cluster
cuts the shelf $4{\times}1$ ratio $6333\to22.1$, yet $6$ of $8$ injecting cells
still overdraw (worst ledge $+1.24\times10^{6}$~J), so band-limiting is a
first-line mitigation rather than a fix.

% =====================================================================
\section{A last-resort guardrail}
\label{sec:bound}
% =====================================================================
When a fixed host cannot converge the row and neither the implicit realization
nor more iterations are available, a deliberately minimal fail-safe holds
\eqref{eq:invariant} regardless of the contact solve.

\paragraph*{Enforcement.} A reservoir $B$ accumulates the supply and is debited
by realized storage, both after the contact solve within the same substep,
since $\dErig$ is not observable until the velocity solve finalizes the rigid
velocities. The substep credits $B \leftarrow B + \eta\max(\dErig,0)$, tests
realized modal energy against $\bar{E}=\Emod^{-}+B$, projects into
$\{\Emod\le\bar{E}\}$ if it would overdraw, then debits
$B \leftarrow \max(B - \max(\Delta\Emod,0),\,0)$ ($\Emod^{\mp}$ are the modal
energies before and after the solve).

\emph{Which} admissible point is free, and the choice matters: scaling the whole
state shrinks the load-bearing sag $\mathbf{U}_y^{\!\top}\mathbf{q}$ that
resting bodies stand on, lifting the support into them (\S\ref{sec:validity}),
so we project along directions the active rows cannot see. Let
$\mathbf{U}_c$ collect the support rows whose gap has closed,
$\mathbf{d}=\mathbf{U}_c\mathbf{q}$, and
$\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{qs}}=\mathbf{K}^{-1}\mathbf{U}_c^{\!\top}\mathbf{y}$ the
least-elastic-energy state with the same $\mathbf{d}$, where
$(\mathbf{U}_c\mathbf{K}^{-1}\mathbf{U}_c^{\!\top})\mathbf{y}=\mathbf{d}$
(pseudo-inverted where the engaged rows outnumber $r$) and
$E_{\mathrm{qs}}=\tfrac12\mathbf{d}^{\!\top}\mathbf{y}$. The remainder
$\mathbf{q}_{\!\perp}=\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{qs}}$ satisfies
$\mathbf{U}_c\mathbf{q}_{\!\perp}=\mathbf{0}$ and
$\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{qs}}^{\!\top}\mathbf{K}\mathbf{q}_{\!\perp}=0$, so
\begin{equation}
(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}}) \;\leftarrow\;
  (\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{qs}}+s\,\mathbf{q}_{\!\perp},\;\; s\,\dot{\mathbf{q}}),
\qquad
s \;=\; \min\!\left(1,\;
  \sqrt{\frac{\bar{E}-E_{\mathrm{qs}}}{\Emod^{+}-E_{\mathrm{qs}}}}\right)
\label{eq:gamma}
\end{equation}
leaves $\mathbf{U}_c\mathbf{q}$ exactly unchanged while landing on $\bar{E}$.
If $E_{\mathrm{qs}}>\bar{E}$ the observed surface is itself unaffordable: the
deepest-engaged prefix of rows that does fit is preserved instead (a
bisection, $E_{\mathrm{qs}}$ being monotone in the row set), failing which the
state falls back to the always-feasible
$(\beta\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{qs}},\mathbf{0})$,
$\beta=\sqrt{\bar{E}/E_{\mathrm{qs}}}$. With no active row,
$\mathbf{q}_{\mathrm{qs}}=\mathbf{0}$ and \eqref{eq:gamma} is the whole-state
scale $\gamma=\sqrt{\bar{E}/\Emod^{+}}$.

All three hosts run this loop identically once $\dErig$ is formed from
\eqref{eq:derig}. Contact is not re-solved and the active set is read from
geometry alone, so no host-specific multiplier is needed, and the projection is
inert within budget ($s{=}1$, bit-identical trajectories).

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:guarantee}
For any $\eta\in(0,1]$ and any host, the loop maintains $B\ge0$ and guarantees
\eqref{eq:invariant} unconditionally, assuming nothing about the contact solve
beyond the projection being the last write to $(\mathbf{q},\dot{\mathbf{q}})$
in the substep, up to an accounting tolerance $n\epsilon$ over $n$ substeps
($\epsilon$ the per-test tolerance, $10^{-12}$~J).
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Carry two invariants over substeps, with $c_k=\eta\max(\dErig^{\,k},0)$:
$B_k\ge0$ and $(\Emod^{k}-\Emod^{0})+B_k\le\sum_{j\le k}c_j$ (both hold at
$k{=}0$). Crediting $c_k$ before the test caps realized storage at
$\Emod^{-}+B_{k-1}+c_k$, so $\Delta\Emod\le B_{k-1}+c_k$; the debit keeps
$B_k\ge0$, and both invariants follow by induction. Since $B_n\ge0$, this is
\eqref{eq:invariant} itself rather than a relaxation, the same-substep credit
absorbing the granularity term a naive telescoping would leave. The argument
uses only that the projected state lands in $\{\Emod\le\bar{E}\}$, never the
direction it moves, leaving \eqref{eq:gamma} free to preserve the surface.
\end{proof}

\paragraph*{The governor holds.} With the governor on, all $72$ sweep
executions and the $18$ deployed cells of \S\ref{sec:kconv} satisfy
\eqref{eq:invariant}: $90$ governed cells ($78$ distinct, the implicit
relaxation pairs being bit-identical) at the roundoff floor (worst margin
$3.6\times10^{-15}$~J).
Preserving the surface stores what the bound permits rather than the least it
can, so the worst realized ratio is $1.15$ (position-based) and $1.70$
(augmented-Lagrangian) against $1.21$ and $1.31$ scaled, the invariant holding
in both.

\subsection{The cost of enforcement}
\label{sec:validity}

\emph{unclamped} = governor off (the truncated solve's own penetration),
\emph{scaled} = whole-state projection, \emph{preserved} = \eqref{eq:gamma}.
Clamp count, impulse (next substep's normal impulse over the unclamped
steady-state median) and $\lambda$ variance (over the engaged support rows,
relative to the unclamped arm) are the preserving arm's; $4{\times}1$ clamps

\paragraph*{Accuracy.} Bounding the energy helps only if the bounded solution
improves on the unbounded one. At a moderate injecting cell (shelf,
$8{\times}2$, relaxation $0.7$) peak modal energy is $1555.6$~J ungoverned and
$28.7$~J governed against the implicit reference's $7.92$~J, an energy error
falling $196{\times}\!\to\!3.6{\times}$. The trajectory still degrades, though far
less than under a whole-state scale: $\|d-d^{\text{ref}}\|_\infty$ rises
$6.5\!\to\!9.2$~mm ($33\!\to\!46\%$ of the reference peak) against $14.2$~mm
($71\%$) scaled. The governor is a safety envelope, not an accuracy device.

This is also why a $196\times$ energy error coexists with a peak deflection
only $1.2\times$ too large: $99.6\%$ of the excess sits in the stiff mode
cluster above $20$~kHz ($83\times$ this cell's $240$~Hz substep rate). A
whole-state scale cannot separate that from the legitimate sag
($99.6\to97.7\%$ above the cut), whereas projecting along the
contact-invisible directions removes proportionally more ($99.6\to89.8\%$).

\paragraph*{Contact validity.} Any projection that rewrites $\mathbf{q}$ after
the solve moves the support surface without re-solving contact, so it can open
a gap violation. Table~\ref{tab:validity} separates the contributions,
instrumented by wrappers that leave the solve unperturbed (clamp counts
reproduce the independent sweep exactly).

\emph{The truncated row opens the penetration; the guardrail amplifies it.} At
converged budgets no substep clamps and the worst violation is
$0.011$--$0.124$~mm ($16{\times}4$, $32{\times}1$, both scenes), so the artifact
exists only where the row is truncated; at starved budgets the unclamped solve
already opens $0.17$--$8.8$~mm with no governor present. The projection then
\emph{amplifies} that residue: a whole-state scale by $2.4$--$47.6\times$
($21.6$~mm, $72\%$ of the $30$~mm board), preserving the observed surface only
$1.0$--$6.3\times$. The exception is ledge $4{\times}1$ ($17.8$~mm), where the
observed surface is itself the injection artifact that no bound-respecting
projection can keep. Nor does the corrective transient soften: the next
substep's normal impulse is $6.9$--$8.8\times$ steady state, so preservation
buys fewer millimetres, not a gentler recovery (supplement).

% =====================================================================
\section{Fidelity and runtime}
% =====================================================================
\paragraph*{The reduced response against a full-FEM reference.} Modes are worth
using only if the reduced response is faithful. Against an unreduced FEM solve
on the same discrete operator (so discretization bias cancels), the reduced
ledge response tracks the reference as the step refines, but not at the step we
deploy: the peak-deflection ratio rises $0.38\to0.54\to0.79\to0.88$ as $\Delta
t$ refines $1/120\to1/960$ at fixed $S{=}4$, and ring frequency agrees to
$0.4\%$ ($78.0$ vs $78.3$~Hz, the loaded ring rather than a basis frequency)
only at $1/960$, the deployed $1/120$ shifting the recovered ring to
$47.25$~Hz. At the operating point of every other experiment
here the reduced model therefore captures $38\%$ of the reference peak, the
residual at $1/960$ being ${\sim}10\%$ $k{=}24$ truncation rather than coupling
error, and the far-field falloff tracks at Spearman $\rho=0.89$ with no fitted
attenuation. This ladder uses a richer $k{=}24$ ledge basis than
the rank-$16$ ledge of the sweep (\S\ref{sec:matrix}), so it bounds fidelity
from above. The limit is a property of the reduction at interactive steps, not
of the injection diagnosed here.

\paragraph*{Runtime cost.} On the CPU host at $16{\times}4$ the ledger adds
$0.23$--$0.41$~ms on the shelf and ledge, $0.9$--$3.4\%$ of those scenes'
$11$--$31$~ms steps; on the table it does not resolve above run-to-run noise
($+1.35\pm2.08$~ms over $10$ repetitions), so we bound it by ${\sim}1.4$~ms
instead, plus one $m{\times}m$ solve per clamped substep ($m\le8$ here). At the
tight deployed $1{\times}8$/$2{\times}4$ schedules it costs $0.3$--$2.2$~ms, or
$6.6$--$34.3\%$, so the guardrail is proportionally most expensive in the
regime that needs it. These are Python/CPU float64 steps and the percentages
are ratios within this prototype rather than a frame budget: we make no
unqualified real-time claim (\S\ref{sec:limits}).

\section{Limitations}
\label{sec:limits}
% =====================================================================
\paragraph*{Stability is not accuracy.} Where the projection is load-bearing it
still opens contact violations (up to $17.8$~mm) and moves the trajectory away
from the implicit reference even as it moves the energy toward it
(\S\ref{sec:validity}): bounded, not faithful. Preserving the observed surface
narrows that gap without closing it and leaves the corrective transient
unreduced; a load-weighted subspace and one-sided constraints remain unbuilt.

\paragraph*{Scope of the row.} The coupling is normal-only (friction stays
body-local, so scraping and rolling lie outside it) and fixes $e{=}0$. The
bound governs modal storage, not spurious energy in rigid DOFs: in the impulse
realization box--box rows rectify a support ring into net rigid motion, to
which the ledger is blind by design.

\paragraph*{Supply and coverage.} The supply is a gross sum, so energy returned
to the rigid bodies and re-dissipated is credited twice; the opposite-channel
exposure $\sum_k\max(-\dErig^{\,k},0)$ reaches $3$--$32\%$ of supply
(position-based), $0.4$--$27\%$ (implicit) and $102$--$118\%$ on the
augmented-Lagrangian host, whose reservoir is therefore funded largely by
oscillation rather than dissipation. It is also uncapped, so
\eqref{eq:invariant} bounds a run, not a limit. Enforcement is host-side and
single-machine (CPU float64), and with one implementation of each formulation
in one contact regime, any claim that descent-class solvers are passive here is
empirical about this sweep rather than a theorem.

% =====================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
% =====================================================================
For a developer adding low-cost vibration to a stiff prop on a fixed-budget
XPBD host, the decisions are ordered (Fig.~\ref{fig:decision}); the real
question is not XPBD versus another solver but the contact-row weight. Where
the two-way row overdraws, make that weight stiffness-aware
\eqref{eq:overweight} or spend the budget on iterations; only a truly fixed
host needs the cumulative bound, which contains rather than corrects. Modal
state is cheap; a truncated solve is not.
